entries.title: The shortest path is not a straight line
entries.subtitle: Richard Réti · An endgame study, 1921
entries.summary: Four pieces. Two distant goals. A king that seems too late to reach either.
body: Richard Réti’s 1921 study asks White to draw. The king on h8 appears unable to catch the h-pawn, while White’s pawn on c6 looks vulnerable to the black king.

The white king advances diagonally, keeping two possibilities alive: supporting its own pawn or catching its opponent’s. The selected line below demonstrates the idea; it is one variation, not the complete solution tree.
Read this as a small authored experience: an apparent impossibility, a change of perspective, and a resolution. The composer arranges what the solver notices, and when.

entries.title: A society carved into the pieces
entries.subtitle: The Lewis chessmen · Twelfth century
entries.summary: Kings, bishops and shield-biting warriors: a board populated by a medieval social world.
body: The Lewis chessmen were found on the Isle of Lewis in 1831. The Met describes their likely Norwegian manufacture, with stylistic and archaeological evidence pointing toward Trondheim. The attribution is a scholarly interpretation, not an identified workshop signature.
Their figures invite a different reading of chess: as material culture. The objects connect craftsmanship, religious authority and martial imagery with movement through North Atlantic trade routes.
Who carved them? Who bought them? Whose society appears on the board? These questions put makers, owners and circulation alongside the moves.
entries.sourceLabel: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · The Game of Kings

entries.title: A quiet move, a composed surprise
entries.subtitle: George Edward Carpenter · A problem, 1873
entries.summary: A mate in two turns the first move into an act of misdirection.
body: Carpenter’s problem appeared in the Dubuque Chess Journal in October 1873. The position contains a white king on d6, rook on c2 and queen on f3, against a black king on d4.
The key is 1.Qh3! After 1…Ke4, White plays 2.Rc4 mate. The surprising first move is part of the artistic effect.
A composition also has a social life: a named author, a publication and readers invited to discover its mechanism. The journal belongs in its story alongside the diagram.

entries.title: Who gets a seat at the board?
entries.subtitle: Vera Menchik · Player and pioneer
entries.summary: A player’s life opens a larger question about recognition, institutions and belonging.
body: Vera Menchik won the inaugural Women’s World Chess Championship in 1927. Born in Russia, she was a Czechoslovak player who lived primarily in England.
Her story offers an entry into the institutions that determine who can participate and how achievement is recognized. A championship is both a sporting event and a social arrangement.
The anthology’s research question: how did clubs, migration, gender and access shape the lives behind the results? A fuller biography and annotated game are still to be developed.
entries.sourceLabel: FIDE Commission for Women’s Chess · Vera Menchik

entries.title: Before the puzzle feed, the manuscript
entries.subtitle: Manṣūbāt · A research trail
entries.summary: Follow composed positions through the people who wrote, copied and solved them.
body: The WFCC traces artistic chess positions to surviving ninth-century Arabic chess documents. This provides a starting point for investigating manṣūbāt.

Research lead: identify a manuscript, its author or attributed author, its copy history and the rules needed to read one position. Distinguish a work’s composition date from the date of a surviving copy.
Next artifact: a source-checked manuscript dossier with one playable position. This entry is a research brief, not a completed historical account.

entries.title: A travelling game changes its language
entries.subtitle: India, Persia and beyond · A research trail
entries.summary: Trace transformations through objects and texts, while keeping uncertain origins visible.
body: The Met presents the game’s likely origin in sixth-century India and its westward movement through Persia and Islamic territories to Europe. This is an introductory route, not a complete global history.
Research lead: compare names, piece forms and rules across dated objects and texts. Treat origin stories, documented transmission and later interpretation separately.
Next artifact: an annotated route map that shows evidence and uncertainty rather than a single inevitable march toward modern chess.
entries.sourceLabel: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · historical overview

entries.title: Learning, ambition and the limits of expectation
entries.subtitle: Judit Polgár · A research trail
entries.summary: A player’s career becomes a lens on how talent is cultivated and recognized.
body: Judit Polgár reached the world top ten. Her own site presents both her playing career and her work in chess education.
Research lead: examine her account alongside interviews, tournament records and independent scholarship. Separate documented achievements from claims about how talent develops.
Next artifact: a profile connecting a game, a learning environment and the broader institutions of competitive chess.

entries.title: When the meeting place becomes a platform
entries.subtitle: Digital chess cultures · An open question
entries.summary: What happens to chess communities when play, spectatorship and reputation share an interface?
body: This is an open research brief. No empirical findings have been added yet.

Investigate everyday practices: watching, teaching, moderation, engine use, rankings and the movement between local clubs and online platforms. Look for accounts from participants as well as platform documentation.
Next artifact: a small, consent-based interview protocol and a bibliography. Avoid treating platform metrics as a complete description of a community.
